groups.title: React's rendering model and reconciliation
groups.question: In your PERN app, a parent component holds a list of posts and each child shows a like button. When a user clicks like, explain how the change travels through your components and how React updates the page without rebuilding all of it.

followUps.How React diffs the virtual DOM to minim: When state changes and a component re-renders, why doesn't React replace the whole page in the real DOM?
followUps.Unidirectional data flow and why it simp: How does the like button in the child change state that lives in the parent, and why is that easier to debug?

evidence.text: On each render React produces a new tree of elements and compares it with the previous one.
It then applies only the differences to the real DOM, which is the slow part to touch.

notEnough: Only saying React uses a virtual DOM so it's fast, without explaining the comparison.

misconceptions.text: Says React never updates the real DOM, only the virtual DOM.

evidence.text: Data is passed down from parent to child through props.
A child changes the parent's state by calling a function the parent passed down as a prop.
Because state only changes where it lives, any change can be traced back to one place.

notEnough: Only saying data flows one way without explaining how a child updates a parent.

misconceptions.text: Says a child can change its props directly to update the parent.

groups.title: useState and useEffect internals
groups.question: Your component has a counter, and it also opens a live-updates subscription when it mounts. A teammate reports that the counter sometimes uses an old value and the subscription keeps firing after leaving the page. Explain why both bugs happen and how you'd fix them.

followUps.Why state updates are asynchronous and s: You call setCount(count + 1) twice in one click handler and the count only goes up by one. Why, and what's the fix?
followUps.useEffect dependencies and the cleanup p: What decides when your effect runs again, and what goes wrong if you don't return a cleanup function?

evidence.text: Calling the setter doesn't change the variable right away; the new value is only seen on the next render.
Handlers and effects capture the value from the render they were created in, so they can use an old value.
Passing a function, like setCount(c => c + 1), always works from the latest value.

notEnough: Only saying state is asynchronous without explaining why the old value is read.

misconceptions.text: Says the state variable holds the new value right after the setter is called.

evidence.text: The effect runs after render and again whenever a value in its dependency array changes, and every value it uses should be listed.
The function returned from the effect runs before the effect runs again and when the component unmounts, to cancel subscriptions, timers or requests.

notEnough: Only naming the dependency array and cleanup without saying when each one runs.

misconceptions.text: Says an effect with an empty dependency array never runs.

groups.title: JSX, props, and component composition
groups.question: You're building a search page where a SearchBox and a ResultsList both need the current search text. Explain how you'd share that value between them, and what JSX actually turns into that explains its rules.

followUps.JSX compiles to React.createElement — im: Why must a component return a single root element, and how do Fragments help?
followUps.Lifting state up to the nearest common a: Where should the search text live so both components can use it, and how does each one get it?

evidence.text: JSX is compiled into JavaScript function calls that create element objects, such as React.createElement or the newer JSX runtime.
Because a component returns one value, JSX needs a single root, and a Fragment groups children without adding an extra DOM element.

notEnough: Only saying JSX is HTML in JavaScript without saying what it compiles to.

misconceptions.text: Says the browser reads JSX directly as HTML.

evidence.text: Shared state moves up to the closest common parent of the components that need it.
The parent passes the value down as props and passes a setter function to the component that changes it.

notEnough: Only saying lift state up without explaining where it goes and how the children use it.

groups.title: Fetching data from APIs in React
groups.question: Your Posts page loads posts from your Express API and lets users reorder them. Explain how you'd fetch the data in a component, what the user sees while it loads or fails, and how React keeps the list correct when the order changes.

followUps.Data fetching in useEffect: loading, dat: The user leaves the page before the fetch finishes. What can go wrong, and how do you prevent it?
followUps.Rendering lists with key props derived f: Why is using the array index as the key a problem when the list can be reordered?

evidence.text: The request is started inside useEffect, not during render, so it doesn't run on every render.
Loading, error and data are kept in state, so the component shows a spinner, an error message or the list.
The effect's cleanup aborts the request, for example with AbortController, so a component that is gone doesn't get updated.

notEnough: Only saying fetch in useEffect without the loading and error states or the cleanup.

evidence.text: React uses keys to match each list item with the same item from the previous render.
Keys should be stable unique ids, like database ids; index keys break when items are reordered, inserted or removed, and state gets mixed up between items.

notEnough: Only saying every list item needs a key without explaining what React uses it for.

misconceptions.text: Says the key is passed to the component as a normal prop it can read.
